cards.statement: A service with arbitrary-precision integers exposes their full range through Int results.
cards.explanation: Int results use the signed 32-bit range regardless of the implementation language. An out-of-range result should raise an execution error.
cards.misconception: The service's programming language determines the public Int result range.

cards.statement: A service returns a resolver's positive Infinity as a successful Float result.
cards.explanation: Float results are finite double-precision values. A non-finite internal value such as Infinity raises an execution error.
cards.misconception: Every value represented by an IEEE 754 runtime is a valid Float result.

cards.statement: A GraphQL service chooses the internal encoding it uses for its String values.
cards.explanation: GraphQL defines String values through Unicode code points. It leaves their in-memory encoding to the service.

cards.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a service serializes a numeric ID result as a JSON string.
cards.explanation: ID results use JSON string values even when the service stores identifiers as integers. This preserves one serialized form for identifiers.

cards.statement: A service may coerce the internal string "123" to the Int result 123.
cards.explanation: The service controls scalar result coercion when it preserves information. Parsing the internal string "123" as the integer 123 is an allowed Int result coercion.

cards.statement: A service follows the built-in coercion rules when it supplies its own Boolean implementation.
cards.explanation: Implementing a built-in scalar yourself preserves that scalar's prescribed behavior. Reusing Boolean's name means keeping Boolean's coercion contract.

cards.statement: A scalar named DateTime gets its date format from the GraphQL specification.
cards.explanation: The service defines DateTime's format and coercion rules. GraphQL supplies the custom scalar mechanism and lets the service choose the contract.
cards.misconception: GraphQL assigns a standard date format to any custom scalar named DateTime.

cards.statement: A custom scalar's @specifiedBy URL links to a human-readable specification of its format.
cards.explanation: The URL documents the scalar's data format, serialization, and coercion rules so people and tools can consult the service's contract.

cards.statement: A schema may attach @specifiedBy to its built-in String scalar to document a preferred encoding.
cards.explanation: The @specifiedBy directive applies to custom scalars. The spec forbids applying it to built-in scalar types.
cards.misconception: @specifiedBy also documents service-specific preferences for built-in scalars.

cards.statement: Introspection includes unused built-in scalars in the schema's type list.
cards.explanation: Introspection lists a built-in scalar when the schema references it. A built-in scalar with no schema references is omitted from that list.
cards.misconception: Introspection includes built-in scalars regardless of whether the schema references them.

cards.statement: The spec recommends writing enum value names in all caps, such as `READY`.
cards.explanation: The all-caps style is a recommendation for schema authors. A name such as READY follows that style.

cards.statement: A service serializes an enum result using the numeric value in its internal representation.
cards.explanation: A service serializes an enum result as its defined name. Its internal representation stays an implementation detail.
cards.misconception: The service exposes an enum's internal numeric representation in JSON results.

cards.statement: A schema must define at least one field on each object type it exposes.
cards.explanation: Even an object used merely as a marker needs a field in its schema definition.

cards.statement: A schema keeps field names unique within an object type, even when the fields have different argument lists.
cards.explanation: GraphQL object fields are identified by their names within the type. Different arguments do not create separate overloads of a field name.

cards.statement: An implementing object may return `String!` for an interface field declared as `String`.
cards.explanation: Interface field return types permit a subtype. An implementing object's Non-Null String return strengthens the interface's nullable String guarantee.

cards.statement: An implementing field may replace an interface argument's `Int` type with `Float` for numeric compatibility.
cards.explanation: An implementing field uses the same declared type for each corresponding interface argument. Numeric input coercion does not permit substituting Float for Int.
cards.misconception: Compatible numeric input values permit different declared argument types on an interface implementation.

cards.statement: An implementing object may add a nullable argument to a field declared by its interface.
cards.explanation: Interface fields set a minimum argument contract. A nullable extra argument does not demand more input from an existing caller.

cards.statement: In the September 2025 spec, an object uses @deprecated on a field whose interface field has `isDeprecated: false`.
cards.explanation: An implementing field is deprecated only when the corresponding interface field is deprecated. The implementation's deprecation depends on that prerequisite.
cards.misconception: An object's field deprecation status is independent of its interface field's status.

cards.statement: A schema joins multiple implemented interfaces with & in an object's SDL declaration.
cards.explanation: The implements clause lists interface names separated by &. This lets one object declare that it fulfills several interface contracts.

cards.statement: An object automatically declares an ancestor interface by listing an interface that implements it.
cards.explanation: An object type's implements clause explicitly includes its transitively implemented interfaces. The service does not infer those declarations from the direct interface alone.
cards.misconception: Declaring a direct interface automatically supplies declarations for its ancestor interfaces.

cards.statement: A query directly selects an implementer-specific field from an interface result.
cards.explanation: The interface declaration determines which fields a query selects directly. An implementer's extra field is reached through a fragment on an applicable type.
cards.misconception: An interface result exposes its implementers' extra fields for direct selection.

cards.statement: A union may list an interface member to include that interface's implementing objects.
cards.explanation: A union's members are object types. To include several objects that implement an interface, the schema names those objects as members.
cards.misconception: An interface used as a union member expands to its implementing object types.

cards.statement: A query directly selects `name` from a union whose object members define `name`.
cards.explanation: Shared object fields do not become union fields. A query reaches name through a fragment on a matching object or interface type.
cards.misconception: A field shared by union members becomes directly selectable on the union.

cards.statement: A service resolves a non-null interface or union result to one concrete object type during execution.
cards.explanation: The service determines which relevant object type represents an abstract result. It uses that object type to complete the result's selected fields.

cards.statement: The service accepts null as a valid result for a field whose schema declaration is `name: String`.
cards.explanation: A field declared with the type String is nullable, so a null result satisfies its declared type.

cards.statement: A field of type `[String!]` enforces a non-null value for the whole list.
cards.explanation: For `[String!]`, the outer List is nullable, so a null result for the whole list is valid.
cards.misconception: An exclamation mark inside list brackets makes the whole list non-null.

source.title: GraphQL Specification — Combining List and Non-Null

cards.statement: The service accepts `[]` as the result of a field declared as `[String!]!`.
cards.explanation: An empty list satisfies `[String!]!`; these wrappers constrain null values rather than list length.

source.title: GraphQL Specification — Combining List and Non-Null

cards.statement: A schema author creates a valid type by wrapping `String!` in another Non-Null wrapper.
cards.explanation: A Non-Null wrapper must surround a nullable type. Wrapping an existing Non-Null type again produces an invalid type.
cards.misconception: Applying Non-Null twice produces a valid redundant wrapper.

cards.statement: A client may omit an argument declared as `limit: Int! = 10` from a field selection.
cards.explanation: An argument's schema default makes the argument optional under the Required Arguments rule.

cards.statement: The service sets a failed item of an `[Int]` result to null while keeping the other items.
cards.explanation: A list with nullable items isolates an item's execution error to that item position.

cards.statement: A schema author may use an input object as a field's return type when its fields are scalars.
cards.explanation: Input Object types serve input positions. A field's return type must use an output type.
cards.misconception: An input object becomes an output type when its fields contain simple scalar types.

cards.statement: A schema author adds arguments to input object fields to configure how the service coerces them.
cards.explanation: Input object fields declare input values and take no arguments.
cards.misconception: Input object fields accept arguments like output object fields.

cards.statement: A schema author may define an ordinary input object cycle whose chain includes a nullable field.
cards.explanation: A nullable link lets a finite input value terminate an ordinary input object's circular chain.

cards.statement: The service automatically records an explicitly null nullable field in an ordinary input object's coerced map.
cards.explanation: Input object coercion records the provided field name together with null in its resulting map.

cards.statement: In the September 2025 spec, an `@oneOf` input may supply a single field whose value is null.
cards.explanation: A OneOf Input Object's provided field needs a non-null value. Providing a single field with null fails input coercion.
cards.misconception: One supplied field is sufficient for OneOf validity even when its value is null.

cards.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a schema author must declare OneOf member fields with non-null types.
cards.explanation: OneOf fields are declared with nullable types so the client can choose which member to provide.
cards.misconception: OneOf alternatives use non-null field types in the schema.

cards.statement: A valid GraphQL schema includes a query root operation type even when clients use the service for mutations.
cards.explanation: A query root is a required part of schema validity, including for services whose applications mainly send mutations.

cards.statement: A GraphQL schema may use one object type as both its query root and its mutation root.
cards.explanation: A schema uses distinct object types for its query and mutation roots. Assigning one type to both roles violates schema validity.
cards.misconception: Query and mutation roots can share the same object type.

cards.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a service runs mutations through the query root in a schema supporting queries alone.
cards.explanation: A mutation operation fails validation when its schema lacks a mutation root. Validation checks that the operation's entry point exists.
cards.misconception: The executor substitutes the query root when the schema lacks a mutation root.

cards.statement: In the September 2025 spec, SDL can omit `schema` when default root names accompany a schema description.
cards.explanation: A schema description needs an explicit `schema` definition, even when the roots use their default names.
cards.misconception: Default root names permit omitting the schema definition even when the schema has a description.

cards.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a non-root type named `Mutation` needs an explicit SDL schema definition.
cards.explanation: The explicit schema definition prevents SDL from interpreting the ordinary type named `Mutation` as the mutation root.

cards.statement: An SDL document may split its query and mutation roots across separate `schema` definitions.
cards.explanation: An SDL document has at most one schema definition. That definition declares the root types together.
cards.misconception: Each supported operation type gets a separate schema definition.

cards.statement: GraphQL gives a schema's object types and input object types a shared namespace for type names.
cards.explanation: Type names identify types across the whole schema. An object type and an input object type therefore need different names.

cards.statement: A schema may use the same enum type for a field's return value and for an argument's input value.
cards.explanation: Enum types qualify for both input and output positions, so one declared enum can serve both uses.

source.title: GraphQL Specification — Input and Output Types

cards.statement: An object field may use the schema's query root type directly as its return type.
cards.explanation: The query root is an ordinary Object type with an entry-point role. Another object field can use it as an output type.

cards.statement: An SDL `extend type` declaration can replace an existing field's return type with a new type.
cards.explanation: An object extension adds to the existing type. Its added fields need new names rather than redefining a field already on that type.
cards.misconception: An object type extension can override an existing field definition.

cards.statement: A client can read the schema's SDL description through introspection at `__schema { description }`.
cards.explanation: Schema documentation is available through introspection. `__Schema.description` exposes the description attached to the schema definition.

cards.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a client identifies a union membership with a coordinate such as `SearchResult.User`.
cards.explanation: Schema coordinates do not identify union memberships. A union member refers to an existing type, whose type coordinate identifies that type.
cards.misconception: Union memberships have coordinates formed from the union name and member type name.
